newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Oil rally under threat by rising supplies.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Oil rally under threat by rising supplies.

text.p: A lengthy rally which has kept oil prices near six-year highs for weeks is under threat as supplies rise ahead of a seasonal downturn in demand, analysts said.

The International Energy Agency said in its Monthly Oil Market Report on Tuesday that the return of Iraqi oil exports and rising output from producers outside OPEC pushed world oil supplies to a record 74.7 million barrels daily in December, up 1.3 million from November.
The Paris-based energy think tank said producers outside the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries should rise a total 2.0 million barrels per day (bpd) to average 45.6 million bpd in 1997.

"New fields in the North Sea and elsewhere, seasonally higher flows in the Northern Hemisphere and the lack of maintenance activities raised non-OPEC supply to a new high of 45.4 million bpd in December," it said.

Now that Iraq is allowed to sell some oil under a United Nations' limited oil sale plan, it and its fellow OPEC members should produce more than 27 million bpd before the end of 1997, well above the cartel's self-assigned but long-ignored 25.03 million bpd ceiling, analysts say.

By contrast, the IEA revised down its estimate for the rise in world demand this year by 200,000 bpd to 73.6 million bpd, for a 1.9 million bpd rise on the year. Oil demand usually eases in the second and third quarters when heating oil use falls.
"By the middle of the year, inventories should reach the point when prices will really begin to deteriorate," said Leo Drollas, chief economist at the Centre for Global Energy Studies (CGES).
The IEA said fourth quarter 1996 world demand ran 300,000 bpd lower than estimated in its previous report at 73.6 million enabling oil companies to rebuild stocks.
"The latest data shows that supply is not as tight as it has been. One has to ask what will happen when the cold weather ends," said Geoff Pyne, energy economist at Swiss bank UBS.

Just last week oil prices were within sight of repeating post Gulf War highs set in mid-October 1996, but they have come under heavy selling pressure this week by forecasts of milder weather in the United States and Europe.
Beating even the most bullish analysts' predictions, international benchmark Brent blend crude oil averaged $20.30 a barrel in 1996, up 20 percent on the year and was trading at $23.45 on Tuesday.
Fears that the frigid temperatures of winter 1995-1996 would be repeated this winter while heating oil inventories are low has fuelled the prolonged oil price rally.
"Oil prices should return gradually to more normal (lower) levels in the face of rising supply," said Mehdi Varzi at finance house Kleinwort Benson.
The IEA data revealed that stocks of distillates, including heating fuel, actually rose in November, easing the year-on-year stock shortfall.
"We are seeing a straight distillate build-up. The stocks are not as low as they have been," UBS' Pyne said.

OPEC producers, who enjoyed windfall earnings in 1996, are likely to face tougher times ahead and may be forced to study the possibility of cutting their output ceiling for the first time in years, a prospect unpalatable to most of the 11 members, analysts say.
The IEA said demand for OPEC crude was likely to prove 200,000 bpd lower than previously estimated at an average 25.0 million, 1.6 million bpd lower than the group pumped in December.
"OPEC has a definite lack of flexibility now. The prospect of it ever cutting the ceiling is slim," Pyne said.

Ambitious investment in production capacity expansion and a campaign to woo foreign investment has led most OPEC producers to ignore their OPEC quotas and maximise production much to the chagrin of Saudi Arabia -- OPEC's and the world's largest oil producer -- and its fellow OPEC Gulf producers Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates.

The trio are really the only oil producers in the world sitting on unused production capacity but analysts and OPEC sources wonder how long they will be content to mothball supply while other producers pump up the volume.
"I shudder to think what will happen to prices if the Saudis unleash their production might. For now, they have been content with the price but if it falls..." a non-Saudi OPEC delegate said.
